solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

parts.note: a life story written by its own subject, the phrase reading like a wish for independence

explanation.surface: Someone longs for a life of their own, free of others.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests independence; cryptically, 'a life' is a biography and 'of one's own' means written by the subject.
explanation.definitionFit: A memoir-style book recounting the writer's own life is exactly a life story by oneself.

parts.note: being up means in residence at a university, a British usage
tight is slang for drunk

explanation.surface: A student who is tipsy and nervous while at college.
explanation.definitionFit: Tense and nervous people are described informally as wound up or tense, a synonym.

parts.note: deadline is read as a line about a dead person, and in short asks for the abbreviated word

explanation.surface: A question about the time a paper must go to press.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deadline' pretends to be the print cutoff; read it as a line written about the dead, and 'in short' calls for the clipped form of obituary.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper notice about someone who has died is commonly abbreviated in journalism.

clue.text: Succeed with a will in their resolve

indicators.note: resolve here means to break up and rearrange, as a compound resolves into parts

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Heirs determined to come into money under a will.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resolve' looks like a noun meaning determination; it is the instruction to rearrange IN THEIR.
explanation.definitionFit: Receiving property through a testament is to come into it as a successor, an exact synonym.

clue.text: Very big chap who went down to a stone!

definitions.text: Very big chap who went down to a stone!

parts.words: Very big chap who went down to a stone!
parts.note: the Biblical giant felled by David's sling-stone, with went down to a stone sounding like a slimming boast

explanation.surface: A huge man who dieted until he weighed only a stone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Went down to a stone' suggests drastic weight loss (a stone is 14 pounds); it means was knocked down by a slingshot stone.
explanation.definitionFit: The Philistine giant in the Bible was killed by a stone from young David's sling.

indicators.note: feature of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Describing a typical element of English Gothic church architecture.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft's definition 'A' cannot mean the answer; the whole clue defines it as well as hiding it, so it is an all-in-one. Perpendicular is the late English Gothic style.
explanation.definitionFit: Pointed curved spans over doors and windows are a defining element of Gothic church building.

clue.text: One who'd have to change for the dance

indicators.note: have to change says these letters must be rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who must put on different clothes before a dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'have to change' sounds like changing clothes; it rearranges ONE WHO'D.
explanation.definitionFit: A lively American country gathering with folk dancing is a classic example of a dance.

parts.note: literally moving without turning, and idiomatically living honestly after a criminal past

explanation.surface: A former offender plainly staying on the right side of the law.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase works twice: moving in a line without turning, and the idiom for a reformed criminal living honestly.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes an ex-convict who has reformed and keeps away from crime.

parts.note: champions as defenders of causes, away from home as wandering in search of adventure

explanation.surface: A sports team that has won the title, playing an away fixture.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is football; 'champions' means medieval defenders of the weak and 'away from home' the wandering of errant knights.
explanation.definitionFit: Medieval wandering warriors roamed in search of chivalrous adventures, championing the weak.

clue.text: Big egg-producer from nothing, on the way to get wealthy

parts.note: nothing is zero, shaped like the letter O
St is the abbreviation for street, a way
rich means wealthy

explanation.surface: Someone rising from nothing towards riches.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a rags-to-riches story; 'from', 'on' and 'to get' simply join the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The largest living bird lays the biggest eggs of any species today.

parts.note: a stand placed in front of someone giving a talk, while the surface suggests rising in front of the Speaker

explanation.surface: An MP rising to address the Speaker of the House.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stand' looks like a verb; it is a noun, the reading desk in front of whoever is speaking.
explanation.definitionFit: A sloped reading desk holds notes or a Bible in front of whoever addresses an audience.

definitions.meaning: old or inferior horses are called this
as a verb, badgers means pesters or harasses persistently

explanation.definitionFit: Elderly hacks are slangily so named, and the same word means pesters relentlessly.

clue.text: Start playing snooker, getting a series of points

definitions.meaning: the opening shot that scatters the reds begins a frame
a run of consecutive pots scored in one visit to the table

explanation.surface: A snooker player beginning a frame and building a score.
explanation.definitionFit: In snooker the opening shot and a continuous scoring run share one name.

indicators.note: to drop tells us to remove a letter from the word before

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Someone about to blurt out an embarrassing gaffe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clanger' looks like British slang for a blunder; here it is literal, something that clangs.
explanation.definitionFit: A struck metal disc that resounds loudly is literally a thing that clangs.

indicators.note: of indicates a piece taken from within the following words

explanation.surface: Asking what a Venetian painter's canvas depicts.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across CanalETTO PICture; Canaletto was an 18th-century painter of Venice.
explanation.definitionFit: The subject of a discussion or essay is its theme, a straightforward synonym.

definitions.meaning: the name of a book, film or work
a legal right or claim, as to property

explanation.surface: A statement that a given name is correct.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both the name of a work and a legal claim to ownership.

clue.text: Is stout possibly, so doesn't dance

indicators.note: possibly suggests these letters could be arranged another way

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A portly person staying off the dance floor.
explanation.definitionFit: To remain seated while others take the floor is the idiom for skipping a dance.

clue.text: It controls the waves, though the rain is wild

indicators.note: is wild says these letters are scattered into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Sounds like a sea scene where something rules the waves in a storm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waves' suggests the sea in a rainstorm; they are waves of hair.
explanation.definitionFit: A fine mesh worn over the head holds curls and set styles in place.

clue.text: Talks a lot with holy men going east and west

parts.note: a rabbi is a Jewish religious teacher, a holy man

indicators.note: going west means read right to left in an across answer, so this piece is backwards

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for saint, another holy man

explanation.surface: A chatty person in conversation with clergymen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holy men' gives two pieces: RABBI goes east (forwards) and ST goes west, making TS. 'Rabbit on' is British slang for talking at length.
explanation.definitionFit: British informal usage has rabbiting for chattering on and on at tedious length.

parts.note: a rose is something that blooms, and the same word is British slang for a blunder

explanation.surface: Asking about an error made by a woman named Rose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rose' looks like a name; it is the flower, a thing that blooms, and the word for that is also slang for a howler.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for an embarrassing error is the same as a word for a flowering plant.

parts.note: mocks someone, as in taking the mickey, or literally dispatches someone to jail

explanation.surface: Someone escorting a man called Mickey to jail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes the mickey' is British slang for mocking; the phrasal verb also means sentences someone to prison.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both satirising someone and committing them to jail.

clue.text: The mantle of sleep is disturbed

indicators.note: disturbed says these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone's slumber is broken, as if a cloak of sleep were lifted.
explanation.definitionFit: A long fur-trimmed cloak or woman's coat is a type of mantle.

clue.text: Stretch a point and look inside

indicators.note: inside places the second piece within the first

parts.note: a prong is a sharp point, as on a fork
lo is an old word for look

explanation.surface: An instruction to belabour a point and examine it closely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stretch a point' is a ready idiom, but 'Stretch' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To lengthen something in time is to extend or draw it out, a synonym.

clue.text: A couple of scraps for bird

parts.note: spar means a fight or scrap
row means a quarrel or scrap

explanation.surface: Scraps of food thrown out for a garden bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scraps' looks like crumbs; it means fights, and two different words for them are joined.
explanation.definitionFit: The small brown common songbird is a familiar example of a bird.

indicators.note: tossing jumbles the letters into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Flipping a coin to win a painting.
explanation.definitionFit: A religious image painted on wood is a kind of picture, especially in Orthodox churches.

indicators.note: with is a loose signal here: the letters of nod and we taken together are combined in another order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A board agreeing to fund something with a nod of assent.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram signal is only implied: NOD and WE are put together and rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To give a lasting fund or income to an institution is to furnish it with money.

clue.text: Mean to grab one or two

indicators.note: to grab means the first piece takes hold of the second, surrounding it

parts.note: par is an average or normal level, a mean
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A miser trying to snatch one or two of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mean' looks like stingy; it is the average. 'one or two' tempts as a single phrase, but only 'two' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: A couple or a brace is a set of two matching things.

indicators.note: damaged signals that the letters are knocked out of order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Something felled at the time it was harmed.
explanation.definitionFit: Trees chopped with an axe are felled, the past participle of the verb meaning to chop.

clue.text: Eager to know about the Orient

indicators.note: about means the first piece goes round the second

parts.note: ken is a Scots and old word for to know
E stands for east, the Orient

explanation.surface: Someone enthusiastic to learn about the Far East.
explanation.definitionFit: Being enthusiastic and eager are synonyms, as in keen to start.

definitions.meaning: strikes repeatedly, as with a mallet
the nickname of West Ham United football club, in East London

explanation.surface: A football team defeating a London club.
explanation.walkthrough: West Ham United, a London football club, is nicknamed after the hammers of its ironworks origins.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means pounds repeatedly, and the plural noun is a London football club's nickname.

clue.text: Sped too much, and exceeded the limit

definitions.meaning: went too far running, past a stopping point
went on beyond the allotted time

explanation.surface: A driver speeding and breaking the limit.
explanation.definitionFit: Running past a mark and overstepping an allotted time are both described by this verb.

clue.text: Yet it might result from inside information

definitions.text: Yet it might result from inside information

parts.words: Yet it might result from inside information
parts.note: a paradox: a leak or insider tip may produce a top story, though it appears on the outside page

explanation.surface: A scoop that came from an insider's tip-off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yet' points to the paradox: inside information produces a story printed on the outside of the paper.
explanation.definitionFit: A major story worthy of the outermost page of a newspaper often comes from insider leaks.
